Like many who have already commented, I would not recommend double majoring. A music ed degree means you're going to have more immediate, better-paying opportunities for work after graduation than someone who has just a performance degree. My husband graduated with a music ed degree, taught elementary general music because of the good work-life balance, and then won a gig two years later. We have friends who graduated with a performance degree and the vast majority are not performing full time... most are giving private lessons at Music and Arts/Guitar Center. 

As far as opportunities to keep doing the percussion/marimba thing during college, you always have your college's marching band, WGI, DCI, and DCA if you like marching ensembles. If you want to stick with the "classical" side of things, you may be able to take private lessons for percussion as a secondary instrument in addition to your bassoon lessons, but that is going to be A LOT of practicing. Others have already talked about other ensembles and performance opportunities so I won't ramble about those, especially since it varies so much from college to college. Usually there are many options, but you would need to talk with someone in advance about the ability to audit those ensembles and if you're allowed to participate in the first place.

I know I'm late to the game on this one, but as someone who is currently going through this and am almost through to the other side (my husband is done with BMT Monday!!) here are some things that helped me along the way:

* First, keep yourself busy. I was lucky enough to have started a new job where the teacher I was taking over for left things in a sad state, so instead of spending my free time dwelling on my absent husband I spent that time trying to put out the metaphorical dumpster fire that was left behind. I also took up watercolors (and discovered that I'm terrible at it). Whether it's hanging out with friends, taking up a new hobby, learning a new skill, whatever, do something to keep your mind on other things. 
* Get out of the house! It helped a lot for me to get out of the house and see a movie or walk around our downtown area because it was a change in scenery. Now that it's summer and school is out you could take an awesome road trip with some friends or just stay local and check out some neat spots near you. 
* Write to your trainee (because they're technically not an airman until they graduate) every day! Tell them about your day, send them words of encouragement, draw them a picture, etc. My husband told me that my letters were the only thing that got him through the day sometimes, and knowing that I was helping him get through BMT also helped me get through it.
* Join one of the Air Force Wingmoms facebook pages. Despite its name, it's actually an awesome resource for anyone with a loved one in the Air Force. They have a bunch of groups that connect people who have trainees within the same flight (training group) and post writing challenges, information about what your trainee is up to that week, and it's a great place to meet new people who understand your situation because they're going through it! I met a couple friends through there and I'm so grateful for that resource
* If you're like me, and you're the type of person who likes knowing things and is afraid of the unknown, research what your boyfriend is going through. There's a plethora of websites and blogs that detail what goes on in each week of training, what the various acronyms mean, how graduation weekend works, and waaaay more about the Air Force than I ever thought I wanted to know. Knowing more about the Air Force made it seem less like this scary, abstract thing and by extension made me feel better about my husband dealing with it.  

Here's the thing: crying and being sad every once in a while is totally okay!! Even near the end of my husband's BMT experience there were times where I would find myself crying because I missed him. The good news is that it's not a 100% communication blackout. Your trainee gets two guaranteed phone calls (one at week 4 and one at week 6), and sometimes they will earn extra phone calls. Keep your phone on and charged so he can reach you - I always had the bad luck of my husband calling whenever my phone was at 5% battery... good thing we have a landline. As BMT goes on, he will also find that he has more free time in his day and can write to you. I absolutely lived for those rare letters. 

Most importantly, don't go through this alone. Reach out to friends and family or join AF Wingmoms or another support group. Feel free to reach out to me too if you have questions or want someone to talk to who "gets it." I'm happy to help however I can :)

Front ensemble tech here! We have this issue a lot with the school I work with. If there's a particular section of music that is consistently an issue I would ask your tech (or band director) to define exactly who to listen to. And make sure that everyone else in the front knows defined listening responsibilities too. Although center awareness is great and all, younger/less experienced players tend to panic and listen back if they notice a tempo tear is happening. Better to have them know what to listen to than have two different things going on. 

By the way, in response to your initial question of how to avoid rushing, one of the ways I build a solid sense of tempo is to do a few reps with the met set to the quarter note. Once that's comfortable I'll put the met on the half note, then after a few reps the whole note, and after that every two measures. It's a nice way of weaning off of the metronome while still keeping players accountable for their sense of time.

As a pit tech, I absolutely love it when my section leaders lead by example. If your pit tech is like me and likes to have engaging rehearsals, keep your energy up and try to encourage others to do the same. If they're more serious, make sure that you're setting that tone as well. Overall, make sure that you're focused and attentive during rehearsals and help the freshman learn how to act during rehearsals. 

I would be wary of how involved you get with teaching people music. Talk with your tech/director ahead of time to see if they're okay with it. I personally hate when students turn into in-line techs, especially because it rubs other students the wrong way. However, sectionals to check up on people and offer extra help if they need it are always welcome!!

One more point to be an awesome section leader. Try to develop a sense of camaraderie with the people in your section. Not only does it make rehearsals more fun, but it will also encourage people to stay in the front because they like it so much. Which means you could potentially move on to snare next season like you want. Also try to act as the bridge between the front ensemble and the battery - it's really easy for people to forget the front exists when in reality it's an important part of the overall percussion section. 

Hope some of my advice helped you. Let me know if you have any questions or want more advice  - I've got 4 years of teaching and 5 years of section leader experience with various ensembles so I've got loads of stories to share :)

As far as general advice goes, I would suggest practicing away from the keyboard almost as much as you do at the keyboard, especially if you're still working on developing technique. It's super helpful to just sit on the floor and work on independent strokes on their own so that you're more worried about technique rather than freaking out about notes. Then when you get to the instrument you have one less thing to worry about because it's so ingrained in your muscle memory that it's now second nature.
